NARRATOR: Section 4. You will hear part of a university lecture about how plants adapt to dry environments. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.
Test1_Sec4_Full_Voice.mp3
Lecturer: [warm] Good afternoon. Today we're going to examine how plants survive in dry environments and the different adaptations that allow them to cope with limited water.
Lecturer: [clear] Water is essential for plants because it is involved in photosynthesis, nutrient transport and the maintenance of cell structure.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] In dry environments, however, water may be unavailable for long periods.
Lecturer: [clear] So, plants living in these conditions have evolved a range of physical and physiological adaptations.
Lecturer: [clear] One of the most obvious adaptations is a reduction in water loss.
Lecturer: [clear] Plants lose water mainly through tiny openings in their leaves called stomata.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis, but they can also allow water vapour to escape.
Lecturer: [measured] Many plants adapted to dry environments therefore have mechanisms that reduce the amount of water lost through these openings.
Lecturer: [clear] Some species can close their stomata during particularly hot or dry periods.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] Another adaptation involves the structure of the leaves themselves.
Lecturer: [clear] Some plants have small or narrow leaves, which reduces the surface area through which water can be lost.
Lecturer: [confident] Other species have thick leaves containing specialised tissues that can store water.
Lecturer: [clear] Succulent plants are a familiar example.
Lecturer: [clear] Their fleshy leaves or stems can hold substantial quantities of water, allowing the plant to survive periods when rainfall is limited.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] Root systems can also play an important role.
Lecturer: [clear] Some desert plants develop very deep roots that allow them to reach water stored below the surface.
Lecturer: [clear] Others develop extensive shallow root systems.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] These can rapidly absorb water from the upper layers of soil after brief rainfall.
Lecturer: [measured] The choice between deep and shallow roots depends partly on the local environment.
Lecturer: [clear] Temperature is another important factor.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] High temperatures increase evaporation and can therefore make water loss more rapid.
Lecturer: [clear] Some plants reduce their activity during the hottest part of the day.
Lecturer: [clear] Others may carry out a greater proportion of their gas exchange at night.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] This can reduce water loss because temperatures are lower and humidity is often higher.
Lecturer: [clear] Plants can also modify their growth patterns.
Lecturer: [clear] In extremely dry conditions, some species grow very slowly.
Lecturer: [thoughtful] Although slow growth limits the rate at which a plant becomes larger, it also reduces the amount of water and energy required for new tissue.
Lecturer: [measured] These adaptations do not mean that dry-environment plants require no water.
Lecturer: [reassuring] They simply allow plants to use limited water more efficiently and survive longer periods of stress.
Lecturer: [reflective] Climate change is making the study of these adaptations increasingly important.
Lecturer: [measured] Changes in rainfall patterns may expose plants to longer or more unpredictable periods of drought.
Lecturer: [clear] Understanding how plants respond to water stress can therefore help researchers identify species that may be better suited to future environmental conditions.
Lecturer: [measured] At the same time, conservation remains important because plants cannot always adapt quickly enough to major environmental changes.
Lecturer: [reflective] Next week, we'll examine how plants compete for light in dense forest ecosystems. Please read the section on plant competition before the next lecture.
Test1_Sec4_End_Voice.mp3
NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 4. You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to your answer sheet.

NARRATOR: Section 4. You will hear part of a university lecture about the importance of bees in ecosystems. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.
Test2_Sec4_Full_Voice.mp3
University Lecturer: [warm] Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at bees and their importance to ecosystems.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] When people think about bees, they often think primarily about honey.
University Lecturer: [clear] But the ecological importance of bees goes far beyond honey production.
University Lecturer: [clear] One of their most important roles is pollination.
University Lecturer: [clear] When bees move between flowers, pollen can stick to their bodies and then be transferred to another flower.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] This allows many plants to reproduce.
University Lecturer: [measured] In fact, a large number of flowering plants depend on animal pollinators.
University Lecturer: [clear] Bees are particularly effective pollinators because they actively collect pollen and nectar.
University Lecturer: [clear] As they visit flowers, they move between individual plants and transfer pollen in the process.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] This relationship benefits both the plants and the bees.
University Lecturer: [clear] The plants gain a means of reproduction, while bees obtain food in the form of nectar and pollen.
University Lecturer: [clear] There are thousands of bee species around the world.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] They don't all live in large colonies.
University Lecturer: [clear] Honey bees, for example, live socially in colonies containing many individuals.
University Lecturer: [clear] Other species, including many solitary bees, live alone and raise their offspring without a permanent colony.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Solitary bees may be less familiar to the public, but they can be extremely important pollinators.
University Lecturer: [measured] Bees face a number of environmental pressures.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] One concern is habitat loss.
University Lecturer: [clear] When natural flowering areas are replaced by roads, buildings or intensively managed agricultural land, bees may have fewer sources of food.
University Lecturer: [measured] Pesticides can also affect bee populations.
University Lecturer: [clear] Some chemicals can directly harm insects, while others may interfere with their behaviour or ability to navigate.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Climate change presents another challenge.
University Lecturer: [clear] Changes in temperature and rainfall can alter the timing of flowering.
University Lecturer: [clear] If plants flower earlier or later than usual, there may be a mismatch between the availability of flowers and the period when bees need food.
University Lecturer: [measured] This can place additional pressure on bee populations.
University Lecturer: [practical] So, what can be done?
University Lecturer: [clear] One approach is to increase the availability of flowering plants.
University Lecturer: [clear] Gardens, parks and roadside areas can all provide useful food sources if they contain a variety of suitable plants.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] It's also helpful to provide nesting sites.
University Lecturer: [clear] Some solitary bees nest in bare soil, while others use cavities in wood or other materials.
University Lecturer: [practical] Reducing unnecessary pesticide use can also help.
University Lecturer: [measured] The goal isn't necessarily to eliminate every insect-control method, but to use such chemicals carefully and only when appropriate.
University Lecturer: [reflective] Ultimately, protecting bees is not simply about protecting one group of insects.
University Lecturer: [clear] It's about maintaining the ecological relationships that support plant reproduction and wider biodiversity.
University Lecturer: [reflective] So, when we think about bees, we should think not only about honey, but about the much larger ecological system in which they play a central role.
University Lecturer: [concluding] Next week we'll look at another important ecological relationship: the interaction between fungi and plant roots.
Test2_Sec4_End_Voice.mp3

University Lecturer: [clear] Slow-wave sleep, which is associated with very deep sleep, appears to be particularly important for some forms of factual memory.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] For example, learning a list of words or remembering information from a lecture may benefit from sufficient deep sleep.
University Lecturer: [clear] Another stage is rapid eye movement sleep, commonly called REM sleep.
University Lecturer: [clear] REM sleep has been associated with emotional processing and some forms of procedural learning.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Procedural memory involves remembering how to perform a skill.
University Lecturer: [clear] Learning to play a musical instrument or improving a physical movement can involve this type of memory.
University Lecturer: [measured] This does not mean that one stage of sleep is responsible for all learning.
University Lecturer: [clear] Memory is a complex process, and different types of information may be affected in different ways.

University Lecturer: [clear] However, simply studying immediately before bed is not a guarantee of better memory.

University Lecturer: [transition] As the river slows down, its ability to carry sediment decreases.

University Lecturer: [clear] Over time, deposited sediment can build up to form new land.

University Lecturer: [warm] Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at forests and their role in the movement and storage of water.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] When we think about forests, we often focus on trees and wildlife.
University Lecturer: [clear] But forests also have a major influence on the water cycle.
University Lecturer: [focused] The water cycle describes the continuous movement of water between the atmosphere, land and bodies of water.
University Lecturer: [clear] Trees interact with this cycle in several important ways.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] One process is called transpiration.
University Lecturer: [clear] Transpiration occurs when plants release water vapour through tiny openings in their leaves.
University Lecturer: [measured] A forest can therefore return substantial amounts of water to the atmosphere through transpiration.
University Lecturer: [clear] This water vapour can contribute to cloud formation and later precipitation.
University Lecturer: [transition] Forests also affect what happens when rain reaches the ground.
University Lecturer: [clear] Leaves and branches can intercept some rainfall before it reaches the soil.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Some of this water evaporates directly back into the atmosphere.
University Lecturer: [clear] The rest eventually reaches the forest floor.
University Lecturer: [measured] Forest soils often contain large amounts of organic material.
University Lecturer: [clear] This can improve the soil's ability to absorb and store water.
University Lecturer: [transition] Roots also play an important role.
University Lecturer: [clear] They create spaces within the soil through which water can move.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] This can increase infiltration, meaning the movement of water from the surface into the soil.
University Lecturer: [clear] Water stored in the soil may then move gradually into streams and groundwater systems.
University Lecturer: [transition] Forests can therefore influence the timing as well as the amount of water reaching rivers.
University Lecturer: [clear] After heavy rainfall, a healthy forest may slow the movement of water across the land.
University Lecturer: [measured] This can reduce the speed at which water reaches streams.
University Lecturer: [concerned] When forests are removed, these processes can change significantly.
University Lecturer: [clear] Without tree cover, rainfall can reach the ground more directly.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Soil may become more exposed to erosion.
University Lecturer: [clear] In some areas, less water may infiltrate the soil and more may flow rapidly across the surface.

University Lecturer: [clear] They are active parts of the water cycle.

University Lecturer: [warm] Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at how rivers shape landscapes and how water changes the land as it moves downstream.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] A river may appear to be simply flowing water, but over time it can transport enormous quantities of sediment.
University Lecturer: [focused] Three important processes help explain how rivers change landscapes: erosion, transportation and deposition.
University Lecturer: [clear] Erosion is the removal of material from the land.
University Lecturer: [clear] As water moves over the riverbed and banks, it can loosen and carry away particles of soil and rock.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] The strength of this process depends partly on the speed and volume of the water.
University Lecturer: [clear] Fast-moving water generally has a greater ability to transport sediment.
University Lecturer: [transition] Once material has been removed, the river can carry it downstream.
University Lecturer: [clear] This is known as transportation.
University Lecturer: [measured] Larger particles may move along the riverbed, while smaller particles can remain suspended in the water.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] The type of sediment being transported can therefore vary considerably within the same river.
University Lecturer: [transition] Eventually, the river may lose enough energy that it can no longer carry all of its sediment.
University Lecturer: [clear] When this happens, material is deposited.
University Lecturer: [clear] This process is called deposition.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Deposition commonly occurs when the river becomes slower or when the amount of water decreases.
University Lecturer: [transition] These processes help create different features along a river's course.
University Lecturer: [clear] In the upper course, rivers often flow through steeper terrain.
University Lecturer: [clear] The valley may be narrow, and vertical erosion can be significant.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] Further downstream, the landscape often becomes flatter.
University Lecturer: [clear] The river may develop wider bends called meanders.
University Lecturer: [clear] As a meander grows, erosion tends to occur more strongly on the outside of the bend.
University Lecturer: [clear] Deposition is more common on the inside.
University Lecturer: [transition] Over long periods, these processes can change the shape of the entire valley.
University Lecturer: [clear] During periods of flooding, rivers can also spread water and sediment across surrounding land.
University Lecturer: [measured] Repeated flooding can contribute to the development of floodplains.
University Lecturer: [concerned] However, flooding can also create serious risks for communities located near rivers.
University Lecturer: [clear] Buildings, roads and agricultural land may all be affected by high water levels.
University Lecturer: [transition] People have developed several ways of managing rivers.
University Lecturer: [clear] Embankments can be constructed to reduce the chance of water reaching nearby land.
University Lecturer: [clear] Reservoirs can store water and regulate its release downstream.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] But river management can also have unintended consequences.
University Lecturer: [concerned] Changing the natural movement of water and sediment may affect habitats and areas farther downstream.
University Lecturer: [practical] For this reason, modern river management increasingly considers the entire river system rather than focusing on one location.
University Lecturer: [reflective] A river is therefore not simply a channel carrying water from one place to another.
University Lecturer: [clear] It is a dynamic system that continuously moves sediment and reshapes the landscape.
University Lecturer: [concluding] Understanding erosion, transportation and deposition helps us explain both the natural development of river environments and the challenges involved in managing them.

University Lecturer: [clear] Some wetlands are permanently wet, while others become wet only during particular seasons.
University Lecturer: [thoughtful] One of their most important functions is storing water.

University Lecturer: [concerned] That means wetlands can contribute to reducing flood risk.
University Lecturer: [transition] Wetlands also play an important role in water quality.

University Lecturer: [thoughtful] This does not mean wetlands can remove every type of pollution, of course.
University Lecturer: [clear] But under suitable conditions, they can help improve water quality.
University Lecturer: [transition] Another major function is providing habitat.
